newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish panel says stresses challenge of EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: Finnish panel says stresses challenge of EMU entry.

text.p: A report on the pros and cons for Finland of joining EMU focuses more on the challenges posed by membership than on the advantages of joining, members of the expert panel behind the report said.

They told reporters at a briefing that their findings, published on Tuesday, were no more pro-EMU than Sweden's Calmfors report released last year which recommended that Sweden should not join the single currency among the first.
The Finnish report made no recommendation on membership.
"That was not our assignment," said economics professor Jukka Pekkarinen, the panel chairman, adding that his group's report was "not more EMU-friendly than the Calmfors report".
The Finnish report "is quite short on the advantages (of EMU membership), it emphasises the challenges," one panelist said.
High unemployment in Sweden was one of the Calmfors report's weightiest arguments against membership of the third stage of European economic and monetary union from the start in 1999.
Finnish unemployment at 15 percent is nearly double the Swedish rate, but the Pekkarinen group said fighting unemployment must be a key objective regardless of EMU.
"Membership of monetary union or remaining outside is not a solution to unemployment," Pekkarinen said.
The effects of joining or not joining EMU depend on a multitude of factors and the whole issue was "very complex," another panel member said.
The report said Finland had three options to choose between -- joining EMU, joining the so called ERM-2 system or living with a floating national currency.
ERM-2 -- an exchange rate mechanism for currencies not in the first wave into EMU but knocking on the door -- was likely to be just an interim solution, Pekkarinen said.
The two remaining alternatives could bring positive as well as negative effects, the report said.

"All alternatives require a permanent change in the economic and labour market policies based on regulated financial markets conducted in Finland during the post-war decades, the internal tensions of which erupted in rapid inflation and big devaluations," the report said. @

Regardless of whether Finland opted for going in or staying out, the country must permanently adjust to low inflation, sustained public sector finances and sufficient flexibility in nominal labour costs, it said.
In a steady international environment, the new European Central Bank would find it relatively easy to keep inflation subdued and build up monetary policy credibility, it said.
That credibility would reflect favourably on a small country like Finland and help maintain low real interest rates and promote stable growth.

From the point of view of credibility, it would be desirable that EMU would start with a small number of stable countries, the report said. But the efficiency gains of monetary union would be greater the bigger the number of EU countries taking part, it noted.

For Finland it was particularly troubling that two key trading partners; Sweden and Britain, would almost certainly not take part from the beginning. "The (efficiency) gains for Finland would be reduced by Britain and Sweden remaining outside the euro-area," it said.
And in addition, economic cycles in Finland had in the past been out of step with cycles in the countries expected to form the nucleus of EMU-Europe, the panel said.

"In the case of Finland, asymmetrical shocks are the biggest problem with monetary union. The Finnish economy has fluctuated in the near past in a clearly different way than Germany, France and other core-EU countries," the report said.
"There is no reason to assume that this problem would have disappeared. It is even possible that the problem is worsening with deeper integration," it said.
The euro was likely to become a major world currency together with the U.S. dollar and the yen.
"It is possible that big fluctuations will occur in the exchange rates between the euro, the dollar and the yen," the Finnish expert group said.
Such fluctuations could become difficult for Finland, especially since Sweden and Britain were likely to remain outside EMU.
With a floating national currency, Finland would find it easier to adjust to severe economic disturbances by implementing big cuts in real labour costs, the report said.

"The necessary adjustment of real wages can be implemented easier and quicker through exchange rate flexibility than through a general cut in nominal wages," it said, adding this was an argument in favour of keeping a floating currency.

A successful float would nonetheless require that the Bank of Finland committed itself to an inflation target very near the ECB's and this in turn would mean that the external value of the markka over the long term should neither weaken nor strengthen considerably against the euro, it said.

The disadvantages of remaining outside EMU included a lack of influence in European economic policy decision-making, and the risk that international direct investments may shun a country remaining outside the single currency, the report said.
